title: COP31 heads into the weekend as poorer nations demand fossil-fuel language back in 'Antalya Accord'
dek: The Turkish-Australian presidency is testing a final cover text before tabling it. Least developed countries, Panama and the African Group have pushed back, and India is in a small group seeking a later IPCC timetable.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The UN climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, was set to run past its scheduled close on Friday, with no agreement in sight on the main political decision, as the summit's presidency consulted countries on a final version of its cover text, which it calls the "Antalya Accord", before putting it to a vote by consensus.

The presidency wants to be confident the text will pass before it is tabled, and observers expect at least one more draft, with talks likely to run into Friday night and Saturday, according to reports. No time has been announced for the closing plenary. "We won't be leaving the rooms of Antalya until we have that consensus," Chris Bowen, Australia's climate minister, who is leading the negotiations under a co-hosting deal with Turkey, said on Thursday, according to the UN's news service.

## What the dispute is about

The draft released on Thursday dropped every mention of coal, oil and gas, replacing the 2023 Dubai pledge to transition away from fossil fuels with language about a transition towards low-emissions, climate-resilient development. It backs Turkey's voluntary "35 by 35" goal for electricity to supply 35% of final energy use by 2035, promotes carbon capture and storage as a response to overshooting the Paris Agreement's 1.5°C limit, and proposes talks on tripling adaptation finance by 2035 while dropping the $120 billion figure developing countries had sought. It expresses "deep concern" that the 1.5°C limit will soon be breached; Bowen said COP31 would be the first summit to acknowledge the overshoot.

Overnight, the group of 44 least developed countries asked the presidency to put the fossil-fuel phase-out back in, remove the language on carbon capture, welcome the International Court of Justice's 2025 advisory opinion on states' climate obligations, and set 2025 as the baseline for tripling adaptation finance, according to reports. Panama's environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, said "Panama will not lend its name" to an outcome that excuses individual national responsibility, and Nepal objected to the text's lack of ambition and proposed an additional agenda item, according to reports.

"Any attempt to undermine or dismantle multilateralism is a red line for Africa," said Antwi-Boasiako Amoah, chair of the African Group of negotiators, according to reports. France's ecological transition minister, Monique Barbut, called the omission of fossil fuels a "black mark" and said France would fight for "clean electrification", while Vanuatu's climate minister said his country had been singled out unfairly in the text, according to reports. Oil-producing countries strongly resist reopening the fossil-fuel language, according to reports; the Arab Group and Russia had rejected an earlier cover text.

## Where India stands

India is one of a small group of countries, with Saudi Arabia and reportedly China, that want the next assessment reports of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) delayed until 2029, after the 2028 global stocktake of national climate efforts, according to reports. Dozens of countries, including the European Union, want them ready in time for the stocktake, and the latest text links the IPCC's seventh assessment cycle to the 2028 review. Saudi Arabia has said the COP "does not determine IPCC publication timelines".

In India's national statement on Tuesday, Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav stressed equity, the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities, a fair share of the remaining carbon budget, rich countries' finance obligations, and opposition to unilateral trade measures such as carbon border taxes, according to reports. India has not publicly responded to Thursday's draft.

## Why it matters

Finance matters most to India and its neighbours. A UN climate yearbook released at the summit found that adaptation finance fell from $81.5 billion in 2022 to $64.1 billion in 2024. For Bengal's Sundarbans coast, hit by three Bay of Bengal cyclones in under a month, adaptation money for embankments, shelters and warning systems is a practical question.

## What happens next

The presidency is expected to table a revised text once it judges there is consensus. Under UN rules any one country can block a decision, so a deal will depend on whether the least developed countries, small islands and Latin American states accept a text without fossil-fuel language, or oil producers accept one with it.
